analysis.investment_thesis: Gillette India is precisely the kind of business I admire — a dominant consumer brand with zero debt, 42% ROE, 58% ROCE, expanding 28.9% operating margins, and consistent FCF of INR 442 Cr growing steadily. The stumbling block is the 48x P/E, which prices perfection for a business growing earnings at only 9-10% annually; I would need this price to fall meaningfully before the margin of safety is adequate.
key_strengths: Exceptional brand moat: Gillette dominates Indian men's grooming with global P&G backing, making its franchise nearly impervious to local competition
Capital-light economics: capex declined from INR 92 Cr (FY2021) to INR 67 Cr (FY2024) while profits grew — the best kind of business requires less capital as it scales
Zero debt with INR 473 Cr cash; financing cash flow consistently negative as the company returns substantial capital to shareholders
key_risks: Revenue growth of 9.4% CAGR is modest — at 48x P/E, even a modest slowdown in growth would cause significant multiple compression
As a listed subsidiary (75% owned by P&G), strategic decisions are made in Cincinnati, not Mumbai; minority shareholders have limited influence
Premium market positioning makes volumes vulnerable if consumers trade down to regional or unbranded alternatives in an economic slowdown
red_flags: P/E of 48.45x with P/B of 22.26x — wonderful business, but the price already reflects the quality with little margin of safety
P/S of 8.41x for a consumer goods company growing revenues at 9% is expensive by any historical standard
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Gillette India checks nearly every box I look for: brand dominance, high returns on capital (ROCE 58.78%), zero financial leverage, growing free cash flow, and a parent company with century-old expertise in building consumer franchises. The gross margin of 62.96% reflects genuine pricing power — men will not switch to inferior razors to save a few rupees, which is exactly the kind of irrational consumer loyalty that creates durable economic moats. Operating margins have expanded from 21.6% (operating income / revenue in FY2021) to 21.7% in FY2024 with further room to grow.

My hesitation is purely valuation. At 48x earnings growing at 10%, I am being asked to pay a high price even for a wonderful business. My best investments have been wonderful companies at fair prices — and 48x for 10% growth is not a fair price by my standards. Existing holders should sit tight; this is a compounder worth owning for decades. New buyers should wait for a more reasonable entry — I would get genuinely excited somewhere around 30-35x earnings.
